candidates.attacker_control: The token used by `getRoles()` comes directly from untrusted request data: the raw `Authorization: Bearer <JWT>` HTTP header (`AuthenticationDataHttp.getHttpHeader`, used at lines 93-102) or the binary-protocol auth payload (`AuthenticationDataCommand.getCommandData`, lines 87-92). The attacker fully controls the header/payload contents, including the header algorithm field and all claims, because no key or signature check is applied before the claims are consumed.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Verified that with only AuthenticationProviderToken configured, the same raw token is signature-verified during authentication (AuthenticationProviderToken.authenticate -> parser with setSigningKey, lines 136, 200-202) before authorization, so a lone token-only deployment does not expose the bypass; the provider is not the default (`authorizationProvider` defaults to PulsarAuthorizationProvider in ServiceConfiguration line 1105 and WorkerConfig line 390); `isSuperUser` is NOT overridden here, so admin endpoints that call validateSuperUserAccess still require the authenticated role to be a superuser (the forged-role superuser effect applies where checks route through the overridden operations, e.g. validateTenantAdminAccess inside allowTenantOperationAsync). Checked the HTTP/binary original-principal paths (PulsarWebResource.validateOriginalPrincipal, AuthorizationService.allow*OperationAsync 5-arg forms, ServerCnx.invalidOriginalPrincipal and isTopicOperationAllowed) and found they use the authenticated role unless the caller is a configured proxy role, so header spoofing alone did not provide a stronger path. Also checked that all function-worker REST handlers reviewed pass clientAppId/authData and that legacy worker download paths are gated by superuser or tenant-scoped checks.
candidates.impact: Authorization bypass / privilege escalation: an authenticated low-privilege principal (or any principal that can satisfy one of the configured non-token authenticators) can have produce/consume/lookup/function/source/sink operations, tenant/namespace/policy administration, and topic-policy operations authorized under arbitrary forged roles, including configured super-user roles for tenant-level checks, and returns the union of permissions of all roles named in the forged token. Depending on the named role this yields cross-tenant access to messages/metadata and administrative control of tenants/namespaces. Secondary defects in the same method: `splitToken[0]/[1]` is indexed without a length check, so a malformed bearer value can raise ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, and the string-role result is discarded at line 113, which makes the provider fail closed for ordinary single-string role claims.
candidates.prerequisites: Broker (or functions worker) configured with authorizationEnabled=true and `authorizationProvider=org.apache.pulsar.broker.authorization.MultiRolesTokenAuthorizationProvider`; plus an authentication path that authenticates the connection without validating the same bearer token, e.g. TLS client certificates, Athenz, or Kerberos configured as a provider alongside/instead of AuthenticationProviderToken. `AuthenticationService.authenticateHttpRequest` (lines 122-132) tries providers in a loop and ignores individual AuthenticationException failures, then `AuthenticationFilter` stores `new AuthenticationDataHttps(request)` (raw headers included) as the auth data later handed to the authorization provider; a client can also set `X-Pulsar-Auth-Method-Name` to select a non-token provider. Authorization must be reachable for the target tenant/namespace/topic; the target role must exist in the relevant policies (or in superUserRoles for tenant-level checks).
candidates.root_cause: MultiRolesTokenAuthorizationProvider builds a JWT parser with no signing/validation key (`Jwts.parserBuilder().build()`, line 66) and, in `getRoles()`, splits the caller-supplied token and parses only the unsigned header.payload segment via `parser.parseClaimsJwt(unsignedToken)` (lines 108-111). It then extracts the configured role claim (string or list) and returns those roles without any signature, issuer, audience, or expiry verification. Every overridden authorization entry point (`canProduceAsync`, `canConsumeAsync`, `canLookupAsync`, `allowFunctionOpsAsync`, `allowSourceOpsAsync`, `allowSinkOpsAsync`, `allowTenantOperationAsync`, `allowNamespaceOperationAsync`, `allowNamespacePolicyOperationAsync`, `allowTopicOperationAsync`, `allowTopicPolicyOperationAsync`, lines 128-252) ignores the already-authenticated `role` argument and instead authorizes with the roles taken from this unverified token, returning true when ANY of them is authorized (lines 128-153).
candidates.title: MultiRolesTokenAuthorizationProvider authorizes requests using unverified JWT role claims
candidates.trace: 1) A caller that can authenticate via a non-token provider (e.g., presents a valid client certificate) sends a request whose Authorization header carries an unsigned/forged JWT naming a privileged `sub` (or configured role claim) instead of a valid signed token. 2) AuthenticationFilter/AuthenticationService authenticates via the certificate provider (token-provider failure is ignored or a non-token method name is selected) and stores the full HTTPS request as AuthenticationDataHttps. 3) The admin/topic authorization path passes that AuthenticationDataSource to AuthorizationService, which invokes the configured provider; MultiRolesTokenAuthorizationProvider's overrides call `authorize(authData, ...)` and `getRoles(authData)`. 4) `getRoles()` re-parses the attacker's JWT header.payload with a keyless parser (`parseClaimsJwt`) and returns the forged role(s). 5) `authorize()` runs `super.<check>(..., forgedRole, authData)` for each forged role and returns true if any role passes, so the request is authorized with the forged role's permissions; for tenant/namespace/policy operations `PulsarAuthorizationProvider.validateTenantAdminAccess` even calls the default `isSuperUser(role,...)`, so naming a configured superUserRole grants superuser-equivalent authorization for those checks. The authenticated client's real role (the `role` parameter passed into the provider) is never used by these overrides.
candidates.unverified: No code was executed and the target deployment's authentication provider mix is unknown, so the concrete exploit (unsigned bearer token plus a non-token authenticator) was not runtime-confirmed. It was not verified whether this exact provider/issue corresponds to any published advisory, and the snapshot has no git metadata to confirm the exact parent commit. Whether the token's `alg` header value is constrained by jjwt's unsecured-JWT parsing was not executed/confirmed; the signature is not checked either way.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-347 Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature / CWE-863 Incorrect Authorization (authorization bypass)

coverage_summary: Scope reported by get_source_scope: 5,473 visible source files (5,482 root files, 9 sensitive-name/path exclusions, 0 symlinks, binaries skipped; same filters for B0/P1). I focused on security-relevant modules: pulsar-broker-common authentication (AuthenticationProviderToken/Basic/Tls/List/Service, AuthenticationData*, AuthTokenUtils), authorization (AuthorizationService, PulsarAuthorizationProvider, MultiRolesTokenAuthorizationProvider, AuthorizationProvider), broker admin auth helpers (PulsarWebResource), binary protocol auth/original-principal handling (ServerCnx), proxy routing/auth (AdminProxyHandler, WebServer, ProxyServiceStarter), WebSocket auth (AbstractWebSocketHandler), function-worker REST authorization (ComponentImpl, FunctionsImpl/SinksImpl/SourcesImpl, WorkerImpl, API resources), and spot checks of package management, SASL/Athenz providers, and token tooling. I did not exhaustively read the large broker service/ledger/client/IO/SQL/Python/C++ areas; coverage is targeted rather than complete.
limitations: No execution, build, tests, or scanners were run; findings are source-review leads only and not runtime-confirmed.
The snapshot has no .git directory, so the exact commit/date could not be established (approximated from pom dependency versions, versioned docs up to 2.8.2, and blog posts up to 2021-08-18).

Deployment configurations (authorizationProvider value, authentication provider mix) are unknown; exploitability of the selected candidate depends on MultiRoles being configured together with a non-token authenticator.

Most of the 5,473 files (broker service internals, managed-ledger, client libraries, connectors, SQL, C++/Python code) were not read in depth, so an unrelated stronger issue could exist outside the inspected areas.
No external data (CVEs, advisories, patches, sibling runs) was consulted, so no claim is made about correspondence to any published vulnerability.
The AIOOBE on malformed tokens and the discarded single-role result were not exercised and are described as secondary code-level defects only.

rejected_leads.lead: Proxy REST resources /proxy-stats and status registered via WebServer.addRestResources without an AuthenticationFilter (ProxyServiceStarter.addWebServerHandlers lines 226-229, WebServer.addRestResources lines 178-189), exposing stats and POST /proxy-stats/logging/{logLevel} unauthenticated.
rejected_leads.reason: Real gap but limited impact (statistics disclosure and in-memory log-level change), appears to be long-standing upstream behavior rather than the snapshot-specific weakness; weaker evidence and impact than the selected candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: AuthenticationProviderBasic uses non-constant-time String.equals for password/hash comparison and MD5-crypt/apr1 formats (AuthenticationProviderBasic lines 91-99).
rejected_leads.reason: Timing side channel is impractical here and the code matches upstream design; no direct authorization bypass established.

rejected_leads.lead: AuthenticationProviderToken accepts tokens with no exp claim as never-expiring (TokenAuthenticationState lines 344-349).
rejected_leads.reason: Requires a validly signed token without exp; no signature bypass and no privilege escalation; design/robustness issue, not a distinct vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: X-Original-Principal / originalPrincipal handling (PulsarWebResource lines 149-179, 252-321; ServerCnx lines 345-399, 811-846; AuthorizationService lines 346-533).
rejected_leads.reason: Traced the 5-arg authorization overloads: originalRole is only consulted when the authenticated principal is a configured proxy role and both proxy and original roles must pass; non-proxy clients cannot use the header to change the authorized role. No bypass found.

rejected_leads.lead: Function-worker legacy package/state endpoints (ComponentImpl.downloadFunction(path) lines 1286-1319, getStreamingOutput 1268-1284, getListOfConnectors 893-900).
rejected_leads.reason: Download paths are gated by isAuthorizedRole for 4-segment paths or superuser otherwise; connector listing is non-sensitive. No missing authorization check found.

rejected_leads.lead: SaslRoleTokenSigner uses SHA-512(secret||message)-style digest, a Weak Random secret and non-constant-time comparison (SaslRoleTokenSigner lines 40-106; AuthenticationProviderSasl line 98).
rejected_leads.reason: Weak construction, but the secret is per-process and role-token forgery would not obviously cross broker instances; no concrete attacker-controlled path to recover or predict the secret in source.

summary: This is an Apache Pulsar 2.9.0-SNAPSHOT tree (~Sept–Dec 2021 based on dependencies/docs; no .git metadata available). I reviewed the authentication/authorization core, proxy, WebSocket, function-worker REST layer, and broker admin auth helpers, tracing how attacker-controlled request data reaches authorization decisions. The single strongest source-evidenced issue is in MultiRolesTokenAuthorizationProvider: it derives the roles used for every authorization decision from a JWT whose signature it never verifies (keyless parser + parseClaimsJwt on header.payload only), so it trusts attacker-supplied claims. This is a credible authorization-bypass root cause in deployments that use this provider together with an authenticator that can succeed without validating the same bearer token (e.g., TLS/Athenz/Kerberos as one of the configured providers); with token-only authentication the same token is signature-checked at authentication, which limits the bypass. Several other leads were traced and rejected (proxy-stats no-auth servlets, basic-auth string comparison, no-exp JWT, X-Original-Principal/originalPrincipal handling, function-worker download/connector endpoints). No runtime confirmation was performed.
